newsitem.title: UK: Ivorian official sees 96/97 output up to 900,000 T.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian official sees 96/97 output up to 900,000 T.

text.p: Ivory Coast's cocoa production in the current 1996/97 season should be around 850,000-900,000 tonnes including the mid-crop because the weather has not been kind this year, a senior Ivorian diplomat said on Wednesday.

"We will have a crop less than 1.1 million tonnes. We had heavy rains this year and that wasn't good for the flowering of the crop," said Antoine A. Delon, the London representative for Ivory Coast commodities.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) meetings Delon said the Ministry of Agriculture had just finalised the official estimate for the 1995/96 crop at 1.1 million tonnes including the mid-crop.
Arrivals were late this year and their weekly pace would continue to be slower than last year until January or February, Delon said.

Ivorian exporters estimated cocoa arrivals to have reached 285,000-300,000 tonnes by the end of November when cocoa was coming at a rate of 40,000 tonnes a week against 50,000 at the same time last year.
Estimates for last year's arrivals at end-November range between 340,000 and 410,000 tonnes.
Delon also said that Ivory Coast would process some of the mid-crop locally this season but would export the rest.
"We started to process it. But some of the mid crop will be marketed," he said.

Asked whether the slow rate of arrivals this year could have some connection with problems related to the working of the World Bank-sponsored auction system of the Caistab marketing agency, Delon said: "That's nothing to do with slow arrivals.
"These people are saying it because they are against it. The system is doing very well," he said.

Focecasting the Ivorian crop has presented crop analysts with a serious challenge this year as they try to establish whether last year's record harvest is a one-off fluke or the beginning of a new trend.
They say more arrival figures are needed to crystallise the forecasts.
